title: Example
body_md: The set of integers $\mathbb Z$ along with the addition $+$ form a group. The identity element is $0$. Also with the addition, the same is true for the set of rational numbers $\mathbb Q$, the set of real numbers $\mathbb R$ and the set of complex numbers $\mathbb C$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: The symmetric group introduced in Section \ref{sec:permutations-basics} along with the composition of permutations satisfies the group axioms. The identity element is the identity permutation leaving each element unchanged.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: The set of natural numbers $\mathbb N$ and addition \emph{do not} form a group. The reason being that the inverse elements do not exist except for $0$.

title: Definition
body_md:
Given a proper subgroup $H<G$ and an element $g\in G$, the set $gH:=\{gh~|~h\in H\}$ is called a left $H$-coset. Similarly, $Hg:=\{hg~|~h\in H\}$ is called a right $H$-coset.

$gH$ is sometimes called a coset if the subgroup $H$ is clear from the context. When we do not mention whether it is a left coset or a right coset, left coset is the default.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Two cosets $g_1H$ and $g_2H$ are either the same subset of $G$ or disjoint (i.e., $g_1H \bigcap g_2H = \emptyset$).
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: If $G$ is a finite group, any two $H$-cosets have the same number of elements.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Given two subgroups $H, L<G$ and an element $g\in G$, the set $HgL:=\{hgl~|~h\in H, l\in L\}$ is called the $(H, L)$-double coset, or the double coset if the pair $(H, L)$ is clear from the context.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Two double cosets $Hg_1L$ and $Hg_2L$ are either the same or disjoint.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A subgroup $N$ is \emph{normal} in $G$, denoted $ N \trianglelefteq G$, if for any $g \in G$ and any $n \in N$, we have $gng^{-1} \in N$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Given a group $G$ and a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$, the \emph{quotient group} $G/N$ is defined to be the set of $N$-cosets endowed with the multiplication given by $gN\cdot hN=ghN$ for any $g, h\in G$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: If $G$ is commutative (for every $g, h\in G$, we have $gh=hg$), every subgroup $H\le G$ is normal.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: If $G=S_n$, the subgroup $S_{n-1}$ fixing the first element is \emph{not} a normal subgroup. On the other hand, the alternating subgroup $A_n$ (consisting of even permutations) is a normal subgroup of $S_n$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Given a normal subgroup $H \trianglelefteq G$, the left $H$-coset and the right $H$-coset are in one-to-one correspondence. Furthermore, the set of $H$-double cosets is also in one-to-one correspondence to $H$-cosets.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By definition, $gHg^{-1} = H$. Therefore, $gH = Hg$. $HgH = gHH = gH$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: For any $H\le G$ and an element $g\in G$, the set of conjugate elements $gHg^{-1}$ forms a subgroup of $G$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $H_1, ..., H_n$ be conjugate subgroups of $G$, such that for each $H_i$ the double coset $H_{i}gH_{i}$ is equal to either $H_i$ or $G \setminus H_i$. Then for each pair of subgroups $H_i$ and $H_j$ there exists a $g \in G$ such that $H_{i}g = gH_{j}$. Moreover, the only double cosets of $H_{i}$ and $H_j$ are $H_{i}gH_j = gH_j$ and $H_{i}xH_{j} = G \setminus gH_j$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $i=j$, for any $h \in H_i$ the shared coset is the subgroup itself.
    If $i \neq j$, because $H_i$ and $H_j$ are conjugate, there exists a $g \in G$ such that $H_j = g^{-1}H_{i}g$. The left coset is equal to the right coset:
    $$gH_j = g(g^{-1}H_{i}g) = H_{i}g$$
    Notice that the double coset $H_{i}gH_j = H_{i}(H_{i}g) = H_{i}g$. But for $x \neq g$:
    \begin{align}
        H_{i}xH_j &= H_{i}xg^{-1}H_{i}g \\
        &= (G \setminus H_{i})g \\
        &= G \setminus H_{i}g
    \end{align}
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Given a group $G$, a \emph{representation of $G$} is a group homomorphism $\rho_V: G\rightarrow GL(V)$ for some finite (but nonzero) dimensional vector space $V$ over a field $k$. When we do not specifically mention $k$, we use $\mathbb C$ as the default.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A representation $\rho_V: G\rightarrow GL(V)$ is a sub-representation of $\rho_W: G\rightarrow GL(W)$ if $V$ can be identified as a linear subspace of $W$ so that $\rho_W(g)$ restricts to $\rho_V(g)$ for all $g\in G$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: For any group $G$, the map $G\rightarrow GL(V)$ sending all elements to the identity matrix is a representation. When $\text{dim}(V) = 1$, we call it the \emph{trivial representation} of $G$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Given two representations $\rho_V, \rho_W$ of $G$, the direct sum of vector spaces $V\oplus W$ admits a natural representation of $G$ by letting $\rho_V, \rho_W$ act on each component separately. We call this the direct sum of representations $\rho_V, \rho_W$, and denote it by $\rho_V \oplus \rho_W$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Similarly, given two representations $\rho_V, \rho_W$, the tensor product $V\otimes W$ admits a natural representation of $G$ by acting on $V, W$ separately and extend by linearity. We call this the tensor product of representations $\rho_V, \rho_W$, and denote it by $\rho_V \otimes \rho_W$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A representation $\rho$ of a group $G$ is \emph{irreducible}, if it does not have sub-representations other than $\rho$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: A representation $\rho$ of a finite group $G$ is a direct sum of irreducible representations.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: The trivial representation of $G$ is irreducible.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
The permutation representation maps $S_n \rightarrow GL(\mathbb{C}^3)$, i.e. $3\!\times\!3$ matrices with a single $1$ in each row and column and zeros everywhere else.
    \[
        (2 \; 1 \; 3 ) \mapsto \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 1 & 0 \\
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & 0 & 1 \\
    \end{pmatrix} \quad
        (3 \; 2 \; 1) \mapsto\begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 0 & 1 \\
        0 & 1 & 0 \\
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
    \end{pmatrix}
    \]

    You can see that the matrices of the permutation representation act on the basis vectors of $\mathbb{C}^3$:
    \[
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 0 & 1 \\
        0 & 1 & 0 \\
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        x \\ y \\ z
    \end{pmatrix} = 
    \begin{pmatrix}
        z \\ y \\ x
    \end{pmatrix}
    \]

    What it means to be a representation is that the group multiplication becomes matrix multiplication, so just as $(2 \; 1 \; 3 )(3 \; 2 \; 1) = (2 \; 3 \; 1 )$,
    \[
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 1 & 0 \\
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & 0 & 1 \\
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 0 & 1 \\
        0 & 1 & 0 \\
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
    \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 0 & 1\\
        1 & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & 1 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}
    \]

title: Definition
body_md: Let $\rho_V$ be a representation of $G$. The \emph{character} of $\rho_V$ is a map $\chi(\rho_V):G\rightarrow \mathbb C$ given by $\chi(\rho_V)(g) = \operatorname{tr}(\rho_V(g))$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: The character $\chi(\rho_V)$ takes the same value on a conjugacy class of $G$. In other words, $\chi(\rho_V)(h) = \chi(\rho_V)(ghg^{-1})$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Let $f:G\rightarrow \mathbb C$ be a map. If $f(h)=f(ghg^{-1})$ for any $g, h\in G$, $f$ is called a \emph{class function}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The inner product of two class functions $\phi, \psi$ are defined as:
\[
\langle \phi, \psi\rangle = \dfrac{1}{|G|}\sum\limits_{g\in G} \phi(g)\overline{\psi(g)}.
\]
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: The characters of $\operatorname{Irr}(G)$ forms an orthonormal basis in the vector space of class functions.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: For a finite group $G$, $\operatorname{Irr}(G)$ is a finite set. Furthermore, the order of $\operatorname{Irr}(G)$ is equal to the number of conjugacy classes in $G$.
head: environment

label: ft
title: Definition
body_md:
Given a group $G$, the \emph{Fourier transform} of a map $f:G\rightarrow \mathbb C$ is a function $\hat{f}$ from $\operatorname{Irr}(G)$ to the union of $M(\mathbb C^n)$ for all $n$ such that 
\[
\hat{f}(\rho) = \sum\limits_{a\in G} f(a)\rho(a)
\]
for an irreducible representation $\rho$.
\label{ft}
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: If $H_i$ and $H_j$ are conjugate subgroups of $G$ such that the only two double cosets are $H_{i}gH_{j}$ and $H_{i}H_{j}$, then each right coset $H_{i}x$ has a paired left coset $yH_j$ where $y = x^{-1}g$ such that for all $h_{x} \in H_{i}x$ and $h_y \in yH_j$,  $h_{x}h_y \in H_{i}gH_{j}$
head: environment

label: constant_on_cosets
title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $f: G \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be constant on the cosets of $H \le G$ and non-zero on at least one coset. Then $\hat{f}(\rho) = 0$ if the restriction of $\rho$ to $H$, $\rho |_{H}$ does not contain the trivial representation as a subrepresentation.
\label{constant_on_cosets}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The function $f$ can be decomposed as the sum of functions 
\[ f_{xH}(\sigma) = \begin{cases} \alpha_{x} \quad \sigma \in xH \\ 0 \quad \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]
for each coset $xH$. Because Fourier transform $\hat{f}$ is invariant under translation we may, without loss of generality, analyze only the function $f_{H}$. For a given $\alpha_{x}$, $\hat{f}_{xH}(\rho) = \hat{f}^{x}_{H}(\rho) = \rho(x)\hat{f}_{H}(\rho)$ for all $x \in G$. Recall the definition of $\hat{f}_{H}(\rho)$ from \ref{ft}:
\begin{align}
\hat{f}_{H}(\rho) &= \sum_{g \in G} f_{H}(g)\rho(g) \\
 &= \alpha_{H} \sum_{h \in H} \rho|_{H}(h) \\
 \label{decomp}
 &= \alpha_{H} \sum_{h \in H} T^{-1} [\bigoplus_{\tau_{i} \in \mathcal{T}}\tau_{i}(h)]T \\ 
 &= \alpha_{H} T^{-1} [\bigoplus_{\tau_{i} \in \mathcal{T}}  \sum_{h \in H} \tau_{i}(h)] T
\end{align}
where in \ref{decomp} we decompose $\rho|_{H}$ into a direct sum of irreps of $H$. But because each $\tau_{i}$ is irreducible, $\sum_{h \in H} \tau_{i}(h) = \mathbf{0}$ unless $\tau_i$ is the trivial irrep. Thus, unless the decomposition of $\rho_H$ into irreps of $H$ includes the trivial representation, $\hat{f}|_{H} = 0$

title: Lemma
body_md: The Fourier transform of $1_H$ is nonzero only at the irreducible components of the permutation representation of $G$ on $G/H$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition, the Fourier transform of $1_H$ on an irrep $\rho$ is
    \[
    \widehat{1_H}(\rho) = \sum\limits_{a\in H} \rho(a).
    \]
    Notice that the image of $\sum\limits_{a\in H} \rho(a)$ are invariant under $H$ due to the symmetry of this expression.
    
    Let $V$ be the vector space where $\rho$ acts on. Under the action of the subgroup $H$ through $\rho$, one can decompose $V$ as irreps of $H$. We group them into two parts:
    \[
    V = V^H \oplus V',
    \]
    where $V^H$ is a direct sum of copies of trivial representation of $H$ (or in other words, the invariant subspace of $V$ under $H$), and $V'$ is the direct sum of nontrivial irreducible components of $V$.

    We immediately see the following by definition:
    \[
    \sum\limits_{a\in H} \rho(a)|_{V^H} = |H|\cdot \text{Id}_{V^H}.
    \]

    Also by definition, nontrivial irreps of $H$ do not have invariant subspaces since they do not admit proper sub-representations. Therefore, 
    \[
    \sum\limits_{a\in H} \rho(a)|_{V'} = 0.
    \]

    As a result, $\widehat{1_H}(\rho)$ is simply a scaled projection to the invariant subspace of $V$. Whether it is zero depends on whether $\text{Res}_H \rho$ has any trivial components.
    
    By Frobenius reciprocity,
    \[
    \langle \text{Ind}^G_H(1_H), \chi(\rho) \rangle = \langle 1_H, \chi(\text{Res}_H(\rho)) \rangle_H,
    \]
    where $\chi(\rho)$ is the character of the irrep $\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}(G)$ given by its traces, and $\langle\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product between class functions.

    The left-hand side $\langle \text{Ind}^G_H(1_H), \chi(\rho) \rangle$ is nonzero if and only if $\rho$ is an irreducible component of the permutation representation of $G$ on $G/H$. The right-hand side $\langle 1_H, \chi(\text{Res}_H(\rho)) \rangle_H$ is nonzero if and only if $\text{dim}(V^H) \neq 0$

title: Corollary
body_md: If the permutation representation of $G$ on $G/H_1$ has only $2$ irreducible components, the Fourier transform $\hat F$ of the membership counting function $F$ is nonzero only at these $2$ irreducible components. In particular, the equation \eqref{eqn:fourier_inv} applies to $F$.

title: Lemma
body_md: For $S_n$ and the subgroup $S_{n-1}$ fixing one element, the permutation representation has only two irreducible components.

title: Proof
body_md: The natural representation of $S_n$ on $\mathbb C^n$ (by permuting the basis) decomposes as a direct sum of trivial representation and the standard representation of dimension $n-1$.

label: def:inj
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:inj}
A function $f:X \to Y$ is injective if for any $x,y\in X$ different, $f(x)\ne f(y)$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
If $f$ is injective mapping a set $X$ to another set $Y$, 
the cardinality of $Y$ is at least as large as that of $X$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Left as an exercise to the reader.
head: environment

label: lem:usefullemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:usefullemma}
For any $f:X \to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ injective functions, $f \circ g$ is injective.
head: environment

label: thm:bigtheorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:bigtheorem}
If $f:X\to Y$ is bijective, the cardinality of $X$ and $Y$ are the same.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
If $f:X\to Y$ is bijective, 
the cardinality of $X$ is at least as large as that of $Y$.

body_md:
The set $X$ is finite.
